strategy.summary:
Präzisionsteile Lindlbauer KG is a small family-owned machining shop run by its owner. It has 14 staff, and we take roughly 37% of its turnover. Its finances are sound and its credit index is stable, but it is clearly cash-sensitive. It complained about our late payments and asked for payment within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount.

The owner admits the costing is stale and is done by his office manager. He has offered an open-book walk-through.

The price letter on the coupling hub (part:320060) asks +7% from November. This breaches the calendar-year fixing and the 90-day notice in clause #3.1. Cost drivers support only about half of the ask: bar is up, labour is modestly up and power is down.

Our position differs by part:
- part:320060: Lindlbauer is our sole active source, and the qualified alternative (Fuchsreiter) quotes higher. Leverage is limited, so squeezing hard risks supply.
- part:320020: Lindlbauer is dearer than our main source, Ilzauer.
- part:320031: Lindlbauer is far dearer than the Czech main source, Hrvelec.

Performance is weak: on-time delivery is well under target and ppm is above the peer median, though both are recovering.

Recommended strategy:
- Block the effective date contractually.
- Accept the open book.
- Trade fast payment for most of the increase.
- Use the +20% volume on 320060 and a longer commitment.
- Concede a modest, driver-based rise on 320060 from the new calendar year.
- Press for alignment on 320031 and 320020.
strategy.decision_maker: The owner decides personally and is approachable. His office manager prepares the costing. A new sales managing director appointed in 2026 may join the talks, but his pricing authority is unclear.

persona.style: Polite and relationship-oriented, appealing to long reliable supply. Personal and informal, with rough rather than tracked costing. Willing to open its books.
other_traits: sole active source on coupling hub part:320060
uncompetitive on flange part:320031 versus the Czech dual source
historically settles far below its asks

needs.detail: It wants punctual payment and is offering a cash discount for payment within 10 days. Faster payment is the most valuable trade we hold.
It wants relief for real wage and bar-steel increases after years of flat or cut prices.
We are a large share of its turnover. The growing forecast on 320060 and secure quota shares matter to it.
It appeals to many years of reliable supply and responds to respect.

constraints.detail: Prices are fixed per calendar year, and changes need 90 days' notice before year end. The mid-year increase cannot apply.
The owner has not tracked material and energy prices since 2022, so the ask rests on rough costing.
On 320060 we have 100% with Lindlbauer. Fuchsreiter is qualified but quoted above Lindlbauer's ask.
The framework renews automatically unless terminated with 90 days' notice. The exit window is still open for both sides.
Our own late payments and rush orders weaken our performance complaints and give it a grievance.

levers.why: The contract blocks the November date and the mid-year change outright. State this factually, not as a threat.
Its own request for fast payment opens the trade: pay fast in exchange for a smaller increase.
Strong volume growth on 320060 is worth more to it than a price point.
Power fell, contradicting its claim of higher energy costs.
Accepting the open-book offer grounds the price in real figures. Its costing will likely show less than the ask.
Bar has eased since its recent peak, so a fresh fact limits the material pass-through.
It settles well below its asks, which justifies a modest outcome.
Its flange price is far above the dual source, so the case is for alignment, not an increase. This reveals the rival's price, so use it only in a 320031 case.
Its shaft sleeve price is above Ilzauer's, which is the case for holding or aligning on 320020.
The alloy surcharge has fallen recently, which offsets the shaft sleeve material ask.
Repeated complaints on the very part with the price letter support a ppm commitment rather than a price premium.
On-time delivery is far under target. Use it only as a late filler, since our payment record invites a counter.
Its ppm is above the peer median. Use it as a fresh fact late in the talks.

trades.why: Cash need is explicit. Pay within the discount window in exchange for a price step, and give it in the last round of the price talk.
The contract already pushes any change to the next calendar year. Offering two sheets that trade a later date against price can add value.
Planning security for a small dependent firm. Twenty-four months captures this value.
A binding growth volume on 320060, within our need, can be exchanged for price restraint.
Rising defects. A firm keen to keep its standing should accept a tighter target at no premium.
Test it as a trade item rather than giving it away.
Bar is volatile and recently rising. Do not offer a clause at a generous price, and accept only if the supplier demands it.

price_view.reasoning:
There is no should-cost, so margin evidence is thin.
- part:320060: drivers support roughly half of the 7% ask. The rival quote sits above Lindlbauer, so expect a modest increase from the new calendar year. Fast payment and volume can buy part of it down.
- part:320031: there is room for a cut versus the Czech source. Freight and lead time narrow the gap, and pushing hard may make Lindlbauer drop the part.
- part:320020: some room to hold or align toward Ilzauer.

We are about 37% of a small firm's turnover and it is our sole source on 320060, so a hard squeeze risks supply.

do: Address the owner personally and thank him for the long partnership and the open-book offer.
Acknowledge our late payments and commit to paying on time.
Cite the contract clause factually and explain the change can only be considered for the next price year.
Bring our own index figures and offer a concrete term package.
Answer every message, including the payment request.
dont: Do not threaten resourcing or termination.
Do not mock or belabour the stale costing.
Do not ask open questions about its margin without bringing data.
Do not demand long payment terms from a supplier that needs cash.

traps: Citing Ilzauer's outlier quote (quote:7300062, far above current prices) in any way. It is likely an error and would legitimise higher asks.
Using 'since peak' index arguments. They are not checkable and cost trust.
Citing market news on copper, electronics or castings as relevant. They are not drivers for these parts.
Leaning on delivery and quality complaints while we pay late. It invites a counter-grievance.
Squeezing 320060 below a healthy margin when the only alternative is dearer.
Using the new-MD news as a lever. It is noise.
Revealing rival prices outside the part concerned.
Pushing after a declared final offer.
Offering an index clause on rising bar at a generous base price.
strategy.writer_notes: Open warmly and personally to the owner. Acknowledge the long relationship and our payment lapses, and commit to punctual payment. State that under the price clause a change cannot take effect mid-year or on the short notice given, so any adjustment belongs to the next price year. Accept his offer to walk through the calculation. Show that the stated drivers support far less than the ask: energy is down, labour is only modestly up, and bar has eased recently. Offer a package of a longer commitment, a binding share of the growing volume and a tighter quality target. Keep fast payment for the final step as the trade that closes the gap. Keep one fresh record for each later round. On flange and shaft sleeve talks, frame competitiveness as alignment with our other sources, not as a threat. Never mention Ilzauer's outlier quote.
questions_to_ask: Could you share the calculation for the coupling hub you offered, with hourly rate and material, so we can settle on a fair basis?
Which discount would you grant if we paid within your discount window, and would it apply across all parts?
Would a binding volume commitment for the coming years help your planning enough to temper the increase?
Which material grade and supply contracts drive your bar costs, and are they bought at fixed prices?
What steps are you taking against the recurring marking and burr defects, and would you commit to a quality target?
Who on your side, including the new sales director, will lead the price talks?

findings.text: No should-cost exists for any of the three parts, so the margin over full cost cannot be measured. Price room can only be judged from index pass-through, the rivals' prices and Lindlbauer's own past settlements. The evidence on margin is thin. The owner has offered to walk us through his calculation (hourly rates, material), which would fill this gap.

Coupling hub 320060: the 7.0% ask (16.30 to 17.44 from 2026-11-01) is about double what the cost drivers support. Weighted 12-month drivers give about +4.6%: labour +0.90, bar +3.92, power -0.19. That figure is overstated, because bar has fallen 2.3% since its 2026-06 peak and alloy does not apply to C45. The letter also breaches the 90-day notice and calendar-year fixing in #3.1, so no change can take effect before 2027-01-01.

320060 benchmark: Fuchsreiter quoted 17.87 on 2026-09-14 [quote:7200013], above both Lindlbauer's current 16.30 and its 17.44 ask. Lindlbauer won the 2025 RFQ at 18.10 but has invoiced only 16.30 [quote:7100028]. Lindlbauer's price is competitive, so there is little room to cut it. A modest rise of about 2-3% from 2027-01-01 is defensible. In past renewals it settled about 3.6 pp below its ask.

Flange 320031: Lindlbauer is 25.34 against Hrvelec's 19.90 (-21.5%). In the 2024 RFQ it lost at 27 against 22. Drivers give about +4.5% (bar +3.56, labour +0.93). Hrvelec still cut its price 3.1% in 2026 under the same drivers. Lindlbauer's price sits well above market, so the case is for a cut, not an increase. Caveat: Hrvelec's price is FCA from CZ with a 42-day lead time, so freight and lead time narrow the gap.

Shaft sleeve 320020: Lindlbauer is 12.06 against Ilzauer's 11.66 (+3.4%). It also lost the 2025 RFQ, 12.90 against 12.40. Drivers give about +3.9% (bar +2.33, alloy +0.83, labour +0.90, power -0.15). Alloy has fallen 5.5% since 2026-06. Ilzauer's 30.03 quote of 2026-09-14 is an outlier, probably an error or a refusal quote. It must not be used as a benchmark, and it may tempt Lindlbauer to ask more.

Lindlbauer's own costing is admittedly stale since 2022, and power is -43% on 2022. Drivers have still risen genuinely over the year, mainly cold-drawn bar at +12.3%. A zero outcome on all parts is not a fair-cost position. The 'since peak' arguments are not checkable and should not be cited.

supplier_wants: Faster payment (10 days, against a cash discount)
risks: We take 36.9% of its turnover and it has 14 staff: a hard squeeze on margin could hurt a sole source (320060, 100% quota)
Our late payments (43% late) undermine our credibility on price
The Ilzauer 30.03 quote could be read as a market price signal for 320020
Pushing for a cut on 320031 may trigger its exit from that part

useful_arguments.why: Power fell, which offsets part of the increase
It settles far below its ask

open_questions: What are its actual hourly rate and material cost (open book)?
Is Ilzauer's 30.03 quote real or an error?
What are the freight and landed-cost difference for Hrvelec FCA CZ?
Can we commit to paying within 10 days, and what discount would it grant?

findings.text: Very small family KG (14 staff, turnover 0-2 M EUR), run by the owner, who decides personally and is approachable. Costing is delegated to an office manager, and the owner admitted he has not followed material and energy prices since the 2022 peak. The 7% ask is therefore probably built on stale or rough costing rather than a tracked calculation.

The owner offered to walk us through their calculation (hourly rates, material). This is an open-book opening: we can test the 7% line by line against the indices. Energy is down 3.7% over 12 months. Bar steel is up 12.3%, about +3.9% on part:320060, and labour is up 2.7%, about +0.9%. A justified figure is roughly 4-5%, not 7%.

Cash is their pressure point. They complained about overdue invoices and hinted they would 'review our conditions'. They then asked for payment within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount. Our record is mixed: on average we pay 3.7 days early, but 43.2% of invoices are late, 26.8% are more than 10 days late, the maximum is 32 days late, and 7 discounts were taken after the discount period. Fixing our payment discipline or offering faster payment is the most valuable trade we hold, and it is also a sensitivity: the late payments must be acknowledged.

The price letter for part:320060 asks +7% (EUR 16.30 to 17.44) from 2026-11-01 with 35 days' notice. Contract clause #3.1 requires 90 days' notice before year end and fixes prices per calendar year, so a change cannot apply mid-2026. The letter's tone is polite and appeals to many years of reliable supply.

We are about 36.9% of their turnover. Their finances are sound (equity ratio 37.3%, credit index stable at 255, audit grade A), so there is no visible distress, but they depend heavily on us. For part:320060 they are our sole active source (quota 100%). The only alternative, Fuchsreiter, quoted EUR 17.87, above even the requested 17.44, so our leverage on this part is limited.

Operational notes: the plant closes over Christmas and January call-offs are due by 10 Dec. A news item reports a new managing director for sales, which looks like noise but means a new contact may join the negotiation.

supplier_wants: Faster payment (10 days, with a cash discount) and an end to late payments
A price increase on part:320060, citing the April 2026 wage increase plus energy and material costs
Probably volume security, since we are about 37% of their turnover
risks: Our late payments give them a legitimate grievance and a threat to review their conditions
Sole source on part:320060, and the rival quote is higher than their ask
A small owner-run firm may react personally to hard tactics or to having its costing questioned
A new sales MD could change the negotiating style

useful_arguments.why: The increase cannot take effect as asked under the contract.
The owner admitted the costing is stale; use this gently, as background only.
Energy fell, which contradicts the 'higher energy' claim.
Their own request for 10-day payment is a trade opening.
They historically settle well below their ask.
544 ppm is above the peer median.

open_questions: What does their cost breakdown actually show for 320060 and the share of material in it?
Would they accept 10-day payment in exchange for withdrawing or cutting the increase?
What role does the new sales MD play in pricing decisions?
Are the increases also coming for 320020 and 320031?

findings.text: Price clause fixes prices per calendar year; changes need written notice at least 90 days before year end. The 2026-09-27 letter asks +7.0% on part:320060 from 2026-11-01, mid-year, so it cannot take effect as asked. The earliest valid date is 2027-01-01, and notice for that had to arrive by about 2026-10-02, so even that date is borderline.

The framework agreement runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (deadline 2027-04-01). Both sides keep a live exit option through the 2027 renewal talks. Other terms: EXW; 30 days net with 2% discount within 14 days; 28-day lead time; 95% on-time target; EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint.

History: it settles far below its asks. All three parts were cut 3-4.3% in 2023, then held at 0 to +0.3% in 2024 and 2025 despite asks of +1.3% to +4.2%. The gap between ask and settlement averages 1.8-3.6 pp. The 7% ask is roughly double its previous asks.

Dependency is asymmetric in our favour on two parts:
- part:320020: we buy 60% from Ilzauer at EUR 11.66 vs Lindlbauer's 12.06.
- part:320031: we buy 70% from Hrvelec (CZ) at EUR 19.90 vs 25.34, a -21.5% gap.
On part:320060 Lindlbauer holds 100%. Fuchsreiter is qualified but quoted EUR 17.87, above Lindlbauer even after its +7% ask, so the second source there is weak. We own the tooling on all three parts.

The supplier depends heavily on us: about EUR 369k of a turnover under EUR 2 M (~37%), 14 staff. It is cash-sensitive: it complained on 2026-08-12 about our late payments and on 2026-09-12 asked for payment within 10 days. We do pay late (43% of invoices late). The owner admits his costing is outdated and offered to open his calculation.

supplier_wants: faster payment (10 days) and adherence to agreed terms
relief for wage, energy and material costs
risks: Our late payment record undermines our credibility on contract compliance
part:320060 has no cheap alternative (Fuchsreiter at 17.87), so pushing too hard risks a walk-away
A small family firm under margin pressure: on-time delivery is only 82%, and squeezing it could worsen delivery
Lindlbauer is uncompetitive on part:320031 vs Hrvelec, so a price squeeze may push it to exit that part

useful_arguments.why: Contract blocks the increase as dated
Energy fell, contradicting its energy claim
+20% volume is worth something to it

open_questions: Was the notice for 2027-01-01 served in time (by about 2026-10-02)?
Will Fuchsreiter improve its 17.87 quote for part:320060?
Can we commit to faster payment internally, and fix our late payment?
What does the supplier's open calculation show?

findings.text: On-time delivery is well below the 95% contract target: rolling 12 months to 2026-09 at 82.1% vs requested date (88.5% vs own confirmed), after a slide from 94.1% (2024Q3) to a low of 78.2% (2026Q1). There is a slight recovery since then. Peer median is 84.6%, so it sits below peers. When late, deliveries average 11.8 days late (max 21).

Shaft sleeve part:320020 is the worst delivery performer: 75% on time vs requested, 78.6% vs confirmed, 25% late. Flange part:320031 shows 12% late but has 12 rush lines out of 72, so our own short-notice orders contribute.

Quality has deteriorated. Rolling ppm rose from 224 (2024Q3) to a peak of 680 (2026Q1) and is now 544, above the peer median of 457. The scorecard class dipped to B/amber in 2025Q4 with one overdue 8D, but is green again. Recurring supplier-caused defects are missing marking, burr and surface damage, all of which point to process discipline.

The coupling hub part:320060 carries the most defects: 16 QNs, 25 pieces complained, 669 ppm over the last 12 months, and 6 supplier-caused complaints in that period. It is also the part with the 7% price letter. Fee recovery is only EUR 150 per complaint, so the real cost of defects to us is likely higher.

The volume outlook is positive and the forecasts are shared with the supplier:
- part:320060: 17,910 vs 14,920 ordered (+20%)
- part:320020: 21,910 vs 19,160 group-wide (our quota 40%)
- part:320031: flat

The extra volume is a trade lever for price or for a ppm/OTD commitment.

Order history anchors current prices at 12.06, 25.34 and 16.30, all held flat or reduced since 2023. Dual sources are cheaper: 11.66 for part:320020 and 19.90 for part:320031. For part:320060 the supplier is our sole active source (quota 100%).

In the supplier's favour:
- Every 8D is closed, and none is overdue now.
- Part:320031 had 0 ppm in the last 12 months.
- The OTD and ppm trends have improved since 2026Q1.
- Our late payments (43% of invoices) give the supplier a counter-complaint against our performance arguments.

supplier_wants: faster payment (10 days for discount), on-time payment of invoices
risks: Part:320060 is single-sourced (Fuchsreiter only qualified, and quoted 17.87), so pressing too hard on the coupling hub risks supply.
Small family firm (14 staff) for which we are about 37% of turnover: hard performance pushback could strain it.
Our own late payments and rush orders weaken our delivery complaints.

useful_arguments.why: OTD of 82.1% against a 95% target and below the peer median.
544 ppm against a peer median of 457.
Six supplier-caused complaints on the part carrying the price letter.
Recurring marking and burr defects on the shaft sleeve.
The +20% volume outlook can be traded for price restraint or a ppm commitment.
Growing need for the shaft sleeve; quota share can be offered.
The contract sets the 95% OTD target and the EUR 150 complaint fee.
It historically settles far below its ask.
Faster payment can be traded for price, which matches its cash need.

open_questions: What is the true internal cost of each complaint (sorting, line stops) beyond the EUR 150 fee?
How many of the late deliveries trace back to our own rush lines or order changes?
How do the confirmed-versus-requested date gaps (known issue) distort the OTD figures?
What capacity does Fuchsreiter have to take part:320060 volume?

arguments.text: Bar material has risen sharply: cold-drawn bar PPI +12.3% in 12 months, and steel is +7.3% since January. On the coupling hub, bar is about a third of our cost. Together with the April 2026 wage round (+2.7%), this alone justifies roughly +5% on 320060.

Our price on 320060 is still competitive. Fuchsreiter quoted 17.87 EUR in the 2026 second-source RFQ, above our current 16.30 and close to our 17.44 ask. In 2025 we won the benchmark. Moving the part would cost Hollerau more and add qualification risk.

We have absorbed costs for three years. Prices were cut 3-4.3% in 2024 and held at 0 / +0.1-0.3% in 2025 and 2026, even though we asked for increases each time. We are now near 2023 levels minus several percent while inputs are up.

Hollerau pays late. 43% of invoices are paid late, 27% more than 10 days late, and 7 invoices took the cash discount after the period ended. For a 14-person shop that finances our working capital. Either the terms are kept, or the price has to carry that cost.

We are an open, reliable partner. We offer an open-book walk-through of hourly rates and material. Quality on 320031 is 0 ppm over the last 12 months against Hrvelec's 980. We deliver your many rush orders on 320031 (12 rush lines).
Your forecast for 320060 rises 20% (17,910 pcs next 12 months). Securing that capacity in a small shop needs a sound price.

weak_points: The 1 November effective date breaches clause 3.1 (calendar-year fixing, 90 days' notice). We gave only 35 days, so the earliest legal date is 1 January 2027, and notice for that is also tight.
Energy is down (power PPI -3.7% yoy, -43% vs 2022), yet our letter cites higher energy costs. That was a mistake.
The owner admitted the costing is stale and done by the office manager, so our 7% is not built bottom-up. Weighted drivers give only about +4-5%.
Delivery is poor: OTD about 82% vs the 95% target, and only 75% on 320020. ppm is 544-680, including repeated missing-marking and burr defects.
We are dearer on 320020 (12.06 vs Ilzauer 11.66) and far dearer on 320031 (25.34 vs Hrvelec 19.90). We lost both benchmarks, so those quotas are at risk.
Hollerau is about 37% of our turnover, so we cannot afford to walk away.
Cash sensitivity: we asked for 10-day payment ourselves, which signals need.
wants: Payment within 10-14 days, reliably kept; in exchange we accept a smaller increase and keep the 2% skonto
A binding annual volume or secured 100% quota on 320060 and protection of our quotas on 320020/320031
A longer contract (e.g. 24-36 months) to replace the price fixing
Alternatively, an index clause on bar steel instead of a full fixed increase
Fewer rush orders and earlier call-offs
red_lines: No price cut on 320060 while bar and wages are rising
No alignment of 320031 down to the Czech price (19.90); we would rather give up the part
Not below about +3% on 320060 from 1 January 2027 without payment or volume compensation
No higher complaint chargeback beyond EUR 150 without a price offset
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the long partnership and acknowledge the date issue openly: we accept 1 January 2027 instead of November, as the contract foresees. We keep the 17.44 ask (+7%) on the coupling hub, backed by the bar and wage indices and the Fuchsreiter quote, and offer the open-book walk-through. We then signal that punctual 10-day payment and a binding volume or longer term on 320060 would let us move toward about +4.5%. We do not mention energy again.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that cold-drawn bar has risen over the year and that labour costs went up with the spring wage round, and we take both seriously. Weighted by their actual share of the coupling hub's cost, those two drivers support a moderate adjustment, well short of the figure in your letter. Bar has also eased again in recent months and power has fallen, which offsets part of it. The general steel figure is a broad market series, not a driver of this part. We are glad to settle on a driver-based figure for the new price year.

We agree your price on the coupling hub is competitive, and we value having you as our source for it. That is why we want a fair, lasting settlement rather than a move. Being competitive does not justify closing most of the gap to another shop's quote, though. Our reference is what we pay today and what your cost drivers support. Your strong position on this part is best kept with a moderate increase from the new price year.

We recognise that prices have been held for some years and we do not take that for granted. Those settlements were reached by mutual agreement in each renewal, at levels both sides found fair, and they reflected the cost picture at the time. The fair basis now is the change in your drivers over the last year. That supports an adjustment, but a measured one.

You are right, and we apologise: too many of your invoices have been paid late, and that is not acceptable for a partner of your size. We commit to paying on time. We would also like to take up your offer of faster payment against a discount, so that you get cash sooner and we get a price you can live with. We would rather fix this through payment terms than load it onto the unit price.

Thank you for the open-book offer; we gladly accept it and would like to go through hourly rates and material together. We also acknowledge your clean record on the flange and your help with our rush orders. At the same time, delivery and defects across all parts, the coupling hub in particular, are below what our agreement asks for. We would welcome a joint improvement target as part of the package.

Agreed: the coupling hub volume is growing, and we want you to have it. Growing volume spreads your fixed costs and is worth a great deal to a shop your size, so it should temper the increase rather than add to it. We are ready to make part of that volume binding and to extend the commitment, in exchange for a moderate price from the new year.

press: Under our framework agreement prices are fixed for the calendar year and changes need longer notice, so any adjustment on the coupling hub could only be discussed for the next price year.
Your letter mentions higher energy costs, but industrial power prices have actually fallen over the last year, so we would ask to leave energy out of the calculation.
We would gladly take up your kind offer to walk us through the calculation, so that we can agree on a figure built from your actual rates and material.
We would welcome a joint plan on the recurring marking and burr defects and on punctuality, together with a quality target we can both track.
On the shaft sleeve and the flange, we would like to discuss bringing your prices closer to our other sources so that your share stays secure.
